content: The pain experienced by women during labor is influenced by a combination of physiological and psychosocial factors, and its intensity can vary significantly. Most women in labor require some form of pain relief. Pain management strategies can be broadly categorized into non-pharmacological interventions, which aim to help women cope with labor pain, and pharmacological interventions, which aim to directly relieve the pain. The objective of this study was to summarize evidence from Cochrane systematic reviews regarding the efficacy and safety of both non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions for managing labor pain. When no relevant Cochrane review was available, findings from non-Cochrane systematic reviews were considered. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, to identify systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials on labor pain management. The included Cochrane reviews followed a standardized protocol with 13 primary efficacy and safety outcomes. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed by two authors and verified by a third. The overview included 15 Cochrane reviews (encompassing 255 trials) and three non-Cochrane reviews (encompassing 55 trials). The results were presented as comparisons between interventions and placebo or standard care, different forms of the same intervention, and different types of interventions. Based on these comparisons, interventions were categorized into three groups: What works, What may work, and Insufficient evidence to make a judgment. What Works: Epidural analgesia, combined spinal-epidural (CSE), and inhaled analgesia are effective in managing labor pain but are associated with adverse effects. Epidural and inhaled analgesia provide significant pain relief compared to placebo or other interventions (e.g., epidural vs. opioids). CSE provides faster pain relief compared to traditional or low-dose epidurals. Women using inhaled analgesia were more likely to experience side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Epidural analgesia was associated with higher rates of instrumental vaginal births and cesarean sections for fetal distress, although the overall cesarean section rate did not differ. Adverse effects of epidural analgesia included hypotension, motor blockade, fever, and urinary retention. CSE was associated with less urinary retention compared to traditional epidurals, but more women experienced pruritus with CSE compared to low-dose epidurals. What May Work: There is some evidence suggesting that immersion in water, relaxation techniques, acupuncture, massage, local anesthetic nerve blocks, and non-opioid drugs may help manage labor pain with minimal adverse effects. These interventions were found to relieve pain and improve satisfaction with pain relief (e.g., immersion, relaxation, acupuncture, local anesthetic nerve blocks, non-opioids) and enhance the childbirth experience (e.g., immersion, relaxation, non-opioids) compared to placebo or standard care. Relaxation techniques were associated with fewer assisted vaginal births. Acupuncture was linked to fewer assisted vaginal births and cesarean sections. However, the evidence for these interventions was primarily derived from single trials, limiting the strength of the conclusions. Insufficient Evidence: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether hypnosis, biofeedback, sterile water injections, aromatherapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), or parenteral opioids are more effective than placebo or other interventions for labor pain management. Among opioids, pethidine was associated with more adverse effects, such as drowsiness and nausea, compared to other opioids. Authors' Conclusions: Most non-pharmacological methods of pain management are non-invasive and appear to be safe for both the mother and baby. However, their efficacy remains unclear due to the limited availability of high-quality evidence. Many reviews included only one or two trials with outcome data, and the overall methodological quality of these trials was low. High-quality trials are needed to better evaluate these interventions. Pharmacological methods have stronger evidence supporting their efficacy but are associated with more adverse effects. For example, while epidural analgesia provides effective pain relief, it is linked to an increased likelihood of instrumental vaginal births. It is essential to tailor pain management strategies to each woman’s individual preferences, needs, and circumstances, taking into account factors such as the anticipated duration of labor, the condition of the infant, and whether labor is being induced or augmented. A significant challenge in compiling this overview was the variability in outcome measures used across different trials, particularly in assessing pain relief and neonatal effects. This variability made it difficult to pool results and draw comprehensive conclusions. Additionally, some important outcomes, such as the effects of maternal opioid use on neonatal behavior and breastfeeding, were rarely assessed. For instance, only two out of 57 trials on opioids reported breastfeeding as an outcome. The authors strongly recommend that future trials adopt standardized outcome measures, as agreed upon through wide consultation, to improve the quality and comparability of evidence on pain management methods in labor.
